title: Small Bowel Obstruction
subject: Surgery
summary: A mechanical blockage of the jejunum or ileum that presents with pain, vomiting and distension. In low‑resource settings, adhesions, volvulus and intussusception are common. Prompt recognition and supportive care are vital.

sections.p: Small bowel obstruction (SBO) is a partial or complete blockage of the small intestine, usually between the duodenum and ileum. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by plain abdominal X‑ray or ultrasound when available.
b: History of pain, vomiting, no flatus or stool

t.b: Shows dilated loops of small bowel and air‑fluid levels; a single air‑fluid level suggests obstruction, multiple levels suggest distal obstruction.
Detects dilated loops and can identify volvulus or intussusception when X‑ray is unavailable.

sections.p: SBO is staged by clinical severity and radiological findings. The most useful system is the Ranson‑like criteria for strangulation and the simple clinical staging of uncomplicated vs. strangulated obstruction.
b: Uncomplicated: pain, vomiting, no peritonitis, stable vitals
Strangulated: peritonitis, tachycardia, hypotension, high lactate

t.b: Lactate >2 mmol/L suggests ischemia or strangulation; repeat if clinical status worsens.

sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals, the leading causes differ from high‑income settings. Adhesions remain common, but tropical infections and herbal remedies also contribute.
b: Adhesions from prior surgery (≈60‑75% in adults)
Volvulus of the sigmoid or midgut (common in malnutrition or malabsorption)
Intussusception (especially in children, often due to Meckel’s diverticulum)
Parasitic infestations (e.g., ascariasis causing mechanical blockage)

t.b: Differentiates mechanical obstruction (dilated loops) from ileus (uniformly dilated, no air‑fluid levels).

sections.p: The classic triad is crampy abdominal pain, vomiting and obstipation. In children, bilious vomiting is common. Physical signs evolve with severity.
b: Early: colicky pain, nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension
Late: absent bowel sounds, rebound tenderness, tachycardia, hypotension

t.b: Absence of bowel sounds indicates ileus; hyperactive sounds suggest early obstruction; peritonitis indicates strangulation.

sections.p: Investigations are guided by availability. In low‑resource settings, focus on simple, rapid tests.

t.b: Identify dehydration and electrolyte imbalance; hypernatremia or hypokalemia can worsen ileus.
Leukocytosis may indicate strangulation or infection.
Oliguria or anuria suggests hypovolemia; proteinuria may hint at renal involvement.

sections.p: Complications can be rapid and fatal. Red flags require urgent surgical referral.

t.b: Elevated lactate indicates ischemia; repeat if clinical status deteriorates.

sections.p: Management follows a stepwise approach: treat the cause, provide supportive care, and monitor for deterioration. Surgery is indicated for strangulation, peritonitis or failure to improve.
b: Analgesia with paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs if bleeding risk

t.b: Crystalloid bolus to restore circulating volume; monitor urine output.
Broad‑spectrum (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole) if strangulation or peritonitis is suspected; avoid in uncomplicated obstruction.

sections.p: After resolution, patients should be counselled on early signs of recurrence and surgical risks. Prevention focuses on minimizing adhesions and treating infections.

t.b: Teach to seek care if vomiting persists >24h or pain becomes constant.

whenToSeekHelp: Peritonitis, tachycardia >120 bpm, hypotension, high lactate >2 mmol/L, bilious vomiting in a child, absence of bowel sounds for >24h

faq.q: What is the most common cause of SBO in adults with previous surgery?
Why is NSAID use avoided in SBO?
faq.a: NSAIDs impair prostaglandin‑mediated gut motility and increase bleeding risk, worsening obstruction.

faq.q: When is surgery indicated in SBO?
faq.a: When there is strangulation, peritonitis, or no improvement after 24–48h of conservative management.

exam: What is the first step in managing a patient with suspected SBO? — Nasogastric decompression, IV fluids, and electrolyte correction.
How would you differentiate SBO from ileus on plain X‑ray? — SBO shows multiple air‑fluid levels; ileus shows uniform dilation without levels.
What red flag would prompt immediate surgical referral? — Peritonitis or tachycardia >120 bpm with hypotension.
Why is broad‑spectrum antibiotics reserved for strangulated SBO? — Because strangulation increases bacterial translocation and risk of sepsis.
In a child with bilious vomiting, what is the most likely diagnosis? — Intussusception, especially if a palpable sausage mass is present.
How would you manage a patient with SBO but no access to X‑ray? — Clinical assessment, nasogastric suction, fluid resuscitation, and close monitoring for deterioration.
